title: AgenticFlict: ~28% of AI-agent pull requests encounter merge conflicts, highlighting integration challenges in agentic coding
summary: A new arXiv dataset paper, examines what happens when AI-agent-authored pull requests are integrated into real-world GitHub repositories. Using 142,652 agentic PRs from 59,412 repositories, the authors reconstructed and simulated merges, finding that 27.67% of analyzed PRs exhibited merge conflicts. Conflicts were often substantial: conflicting PRs averaged 11.36 conflict regions and approximately 540 conflicting lines. Conflict rates varied across coding agents (15.24% for Copilot up to 31.85% for OpenAI Codex) and increased with pull-request size. The paper notes that prior research on human-authored software development has also found merge conflicts to be common, with some large-scale studies reporting that roughly 20% of merges require manual intervention. However, the datasets, methodologies and repositories differ, so the figures are not directly comparable. As a result, the study should not be interpreted as showing that AI agents create more integration friction than human developers. Instead, it highlights that merge conflicts are a significant and measurable aspect of AI-generated contributions and that evaluating coding agents requires looking beyond code generation and task completion to include how smoothly their changes integrate into collaborative development workflows.
whyItMatters: Agent 'velocity' metrics that count generated or opened PRs overstate real delivery: ~28% of agent PRs need manual conflict resolution, so net cycle-time gains are smaller than dashboards suggest.
Tool choice has a measurable operational cost — a 2x spread in conflict rate between agents means vendor selection should weigh integration behavior, not just task-solving leaderboards.
Because conflicts scale with PR size, the 'one big autonomous change' pattern is the most expensive; smaller, scoped agent tasks integrate far more cleanly.
recommendedActions: Track a 'conflict rate' and rebase/resolution-time metric on agent-authored PRs, not just open/merge counts, to see the true cost of agentic throughput.
Set guardrails that keep agent PRs small and short-lived (scoped tasks, frequent rebasing) to cut conflict probability.
Run an internal bake-off comparing your candidate agents on conflict rate against your own repos before standardizing.
Route high-conflict agent changes through trunk-based or stacked-PR workflows that surface conflicts earlier.
risksAndCaveats: Conflicts were measured via reconstruction/simulation of merges on a snapshot dated January 5, 2026; absolute rates may shift as agents and repo workflows evolve.
The study reports agentic conflict rates but provides no matched human-PR baseline, so the comparative 'extra' friction versus human PRs is not directly established.
Results are a preprint (not yet peer-reviewed) and skew toward popular open-source repositories, which may differ from enterprise monorepos.
